tier_reason: The v0.3.0 GitHub release notes (first-party) carry a table of OpenZL LZ v0.3.0 vs zstd on Silesia (decompression 3062 vs 1254 MB/s, compression 467 vs 419 MB/s) but state no CPU model, compiler, flags or zstd level; the trained-compressor numbers (340 vs 220 MB/s) come from Meta's own arXiv whitepaper, seen only as a search snippet and not peer-reviewed. First-party with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Release notes v0.3.0 (opened): on Silesia, OpenZL LZ v0.3.0 ratio 2.73, compression 467 MB/s, decompression 3062 MB/s vs zstd ratio 2.74, 419 MB/s, 1254 MB/s ("144% faster" decoding than zstd "at equivalent settings"); a Compression Transformer table on 868 numeric stream families (17.9 GB) reports ratio 7.76x vs zstd -19 5.752x and xz -9 5.920x (ratio, not speed). Snippet only (arXiv 2510.03203, not opened): on the PPMF Unit dataset a trained OpenZL compressor compresses at 340 MB/s vs zstd -3 at 220 MB/s with a better ratio; ppmf_person compresses 55% better than xz -9 and 11x as fast.
corrections.caveats: Release-note numbers state no CPU model, compiler, flags, zstd version or level, or benchmark command; the repo's benchmark/ directory (Google Benchmark e2e/micro harness) publishes no results. Trained-compressor numbers come from Meta's own whitepaper, seen only as search snippets (arXiv, engineering.fb.com and openzl.org are blocked here). Gains on structured formats need a format description or training; on CSV compression speed is capped near 64 MB/s by parsing (snippet). lzbench lists openzl as a target but its README table has no openzl rows.

notes: Metadata checked on github.com: BSD license, 3.2k stars, not archived, last commit 2026-10-02 on dev. The LZ-vs-zstd numbers are now sourced from a page actually opened; the format-aware claims remain snippet-only.

tier_reason: Public benchmark harness in lin-toto/recoil-testscripts (Dockerfile with gcc-10/CUDA 12.1, build.sh with CMake Release builds, testscripts/main.py) compares Recoil against single-thread and conventional interleaved rANS and the multians GPU decoder, but its results spreadsheet is an empty template and the peer-reviewed ICPP 2023 paper (arXiv, ACM, ar5iv blocked) was seen only via snippets ("over 90 GB/s on a Turing GPU"). Without readable numbers or a CPU model it cannot reach B or A; C pending paper access.

corrections.baseline: single-thread interleaved rANS, conventional fixed-partition parallel rANS, and the multians GPU ANS decoder (not zstd/lz4/zlib/brotli/xz)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Snippet only (ICPP 2023 paper, arXiv 2306.12141, not opened): decoding throughput comparable to conventional parallel rANS while cutting compression overhead by up to 14.12% vs fixed partitioning, over 90 GB/s on a Turing GPU, greatly outperforming other ANS-based codecs such as multians. No per-dataset numbers read.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc-10 (g++-10) and CUDA 12.1 in the testscripts Dockerfile; CMake Release build with -DPROB_BITS=11/16 and optional -DAVX512 (from build.sh); exact optimization flags not checked
corrections.caveats: Benchmark harness is public (recoil-testscripts: Dockerfile, build.sh, runall.sh, datasets rand_*, dickens, webster, enwik8/9, div2k) but Recoil_ExperimentData.xlsx is an empty paste-in template, so no numbers are in any repo; paper numbers seen only as search snippets since arXiv/ACM are blocked here. Recoil's CPU throughput is only comparable to conventional parallel rANS; its win is lower metadata overhead and decoder-adaptive scalability, and the clear speed win is over multians and single-thread decoding. Baseline is off the zlib/zstd/lz4/brotli/xz list. GPL-3.0: copyable only under GPL terms. A verifier with arXiv access could raise it to B.

notes: Metadata checked on github.com: GPL-3.0, 19 stars, 2 forks, last commit 2026-07-12 (LICENSE added), active. Not rejected: peer-reviewed paper with a public harness, tier C not D.
